records.targetHebrew: יתום מורה על קטנות הדעת, והיינו שזאת הוא ברצון השי"ת שאדם יעבוד את השי"ת עם זה הקטנות הדעת שיש לו, ולא ילך עם התקיפות שהכל הוא בידי שמים. וכן אל יבטל עצמו לגמרי. כן נמי אל יכריח כביכול את השי"ת, ורק יעבוד את השי"ת עם זה הדעת שיש לו, ולא ילך עם התקיפות שהכל הוא בידי שמים. וכן אל יבטל עצמו לגמרי כן נמי אל יכריח כביכול את השי"ת, ורק יעבוד את השי"ת עם זה הדעת שיש לו עד מקום שידו מגעת. וכל זה הוא בהוה מוכרח להיות מעט הסתרה, כדי שיהיה מקום לעבודה, אבל על העבר שגבר על האדם ההסתר ולאחר התשובה שפונה עצמו להשי"ת, אז מראה לו השי"ת כנ"ל שגדולה תשובה שמגעת עד כסא הכבוד. וכן שזדונות נעשות לו כזכיות, שזה הכל מורה שגם בעת ההסתר היה מקושר עם השי"ת:
records.targetEnglish: An orphan signifies limited understanding. God desires that a person serve Him with the limited understanding he has. He should not proceed with the confidence that everything is in Heaven’s hands, nor nullify himself entirely, nor, as it were, force God. He should serve God with the understanding he has. He should not proceed with the confidence that everything is in Heaven’s hands, nor nullify himself entirely, nor, as it were, force God, but serve Him with the understanding he has, as far as his ability reaches. All this requires a measure of concealment in the present, so that there can be a place for service. But concerning the past, when concealment overcame the person, after his repentance and turning toward God, God shows him what was explained: repentance is great, reaching the Throne of Glory, and deliberate sins become merits. All this shows that even during the concealment he was bound to God.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef expressly separates the past recognized after repentance from the present in which a person must work with his actual understanding. That distinction safeguards the meaning of Chanukah’s retrospective clarification. Knowledge that the bond endured does not excuse abandoning present judgment, effort, or the choice to return. The repetition in the translation follows the unchanged canonical paragraph.

records.originHebrew: וְזֶה נִרְמָז בְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (סוֹף עֵדֻיּוֹת) שֶׁאֵלִיָּהוּ בָּא לַעֲשׂוֹת שָׁלוֹם בָּעוֹלָם; וְהַיְנוּ הַשָּׁלוֹם מֵעִקַּר הַמִּלְחָמָה הַפְּנִימִית כְּנֶגֶד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשֵׁם רַבֵּנוּ רַבִּי בִּינֶם זְכַר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה שֶׁאָמַר: שֶׁפֵּרוּשׁ הַפָּשׁוּט בְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "כִּי תֵצֵא לַמִּלְחָמָה עַל אֹיְבֶךָ" הוּא עַל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁנִּקְרָא "אוֹיֵב" וְ"שׂוֹנֵא", וְאֵין זֶה דֶּרֶךְ דְּרָשׁ וְרֶמֶז; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ בְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אֵין שָׁלוֹם בַּעֲצָמַי מִפְּנֵי חַטָּאתִי", שֶׁעִקַּר הַפֵּרוּד וּמִלְחָמָה הוּא בְּגוּף הָאָדָם בֵּין עַצְמוֹתָיו עַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא וְהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וּמִמֵּילָא מִסְתַּעֵף הַמִּלְחָמָה מִבַּחוּץ, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם קִטְרוּג כְּשֶׁמּוֹצְאִין שֶׁהַיִּשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לוֹ עֵסֶק וּמִלְחָמָה פְּנִימִית; וְאֵלִיָּהוּ בָּא לַעֲשׂוֹת שָׁלוֹם, שֶׁיַּכְנִיס הִרְהוּרֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵמָה בְּלֵב כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְיִהְיֶה שָׁלוֹם בֵּינֵיהֶם מִכָּל הָעִנְיָנִים, וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְהֵשִׁיב לֵב וְגוֹמֵר".
records.originEnglish: This is hinted at in the statement at the end of Eduyot that Elijah comes to make peace in the world. It means peace from the principal inward war against the evil inclination. In the name of our teacher Rabbi Bunim of blessed memory it was said that the plain meaning of “When you go out to war against your enemies” concerns the evil inclination, called “enemy” and “hater”; this is not merely a homiletical allusion. As we have explained concerning “There is no peace in my bones because of my sin,” the principal division and war is within a person’s body, between his bones, through sin and the evil inclination. From this external war branches out: the accusers have a claim when they find an Israelite occupied in an inward war. Elijah comes to make peace by placing thoughts of full repentance into every Israelite heart, so that there will be peace among them in every respect. This is “He will return the heart...”
records.themeTitle: External peace begins with the repair of the inward conflict
records.themeSummary: The ois interprets Elijah’s peace through repentance that resolves the war within the person. The relation between inner repair and outward deliverance is therefore causal, with complete peace still presented as Elijah’s future work.
records.targetHebrew: וְשֹׁרֶשׁ הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּהוּא הַחֲרָטָה מֵהַחֵטְא וּשְׁמִירָה מִמֶּנּוּ לְהַבָּא — הִנֵּה קַבָּלַת הַשְּׁמִירָה מִגּוּף הַחֵטְא עַצְמוֹ מֵבִיא רְפוּאָה לְמַכַּת הַחֵטְא, וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ הוּא קַבָּלַת גְּדֵרִים וּסְיָיגִים עַל עֶצֶם הַדָּבָר שֶׁסְּבִיבוֹת הַחֵטְא, שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא לִידֵי חֵטְא — זֶהוּ הַגּוֹרֵם גְּאֻלָּה וְנִיצּוּחַ לָאֻמָּה הַמְשֻׁעְבֶּדֶת, בִּהְיוֹתוֹ מִתְרַחֵק עַל יְדֵי זֶה מֵהַחֵטְא לְגַמְרֵי
records.targetEnglish: The root of repentance is regret for the sin and guarding against it in the future. Accepting the obligation to guard against the sin itself brings healing to the wound of sin. Its extension is accepting boundaries and safeguards around the matter surrounding the sin, so as not to come to sin. This is what brings deliverance and victory over the subjugating nation, because through it the person distances himself entirely from the sin.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin identifies the practical extension of inner repair: safeguards prevent the outward conditions of bondage from carrying a person back into the sin. This makes concrete the origin’s claim that external conflict branches from the inward conflict. Its full paragraph distinguishes this real but still reversible deliverance from the final repair of the root; it does not equate an initial victory with Elijah’s complete peace.

records.originHebrew: וְאִיתָא (סוֹף סוֹטָה): "וַחֲסִידוּת מְבִיאָה לִידֵי רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ מְבִיאָה לִידֵי תְּחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים, וּתְחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים בָּא עַל יְדֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ הַנָּבִיא זָכוּר לַטּוֹב", וְזֶה גַּם כֵּן מְרַמֵּז עַל זֶה: שֶׁאֵלִיָּהוּ הַנָּבִיא יַחֲזִיר בִּתְשׁוּבָה אַף הַפּוֹשְׁעִים, רְשָׁעִים שֶׁבְּחַיֵּיהֶן קְרוּיִם "מֵתִים" כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרָכוֹת י״ח עַמּוּד ב׳), וְהוּא יַחֲזִירֵם בִּתְשׁוּבָה וִיחַיֶּה אוֹתָם, וְזֶה גַּם כֵּן בְּחִינַת תְּחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים.
records.originEnglish: At the end of Sotah it says: “Piety brings to the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit brings to the resurrection of the dead, and the resurrection of the dead comes through Elijah the prophet, remembered for good.” This too alludes to the matter: Elijah will bring even the transgressors back in repentance—the wicked, who even in their lifetimes are called “dead,” as stated in Berakhot. He will bring them back and give them life. This too is an aspect of the resurrection of the dead.
records.themeTitle: Elijah’s life is the point from which renewal can begin
records.themeSummary: The ois links Elijah’s future resurrection with the present meaning of reviving a person through repentance. Its further account of Torah’s dew places this renewal in a life deeper than the state that appears dead.
records.targetHebrew: היינו כי אליהו הוא ההבלא דגרמי מכל ישראל כי כמו שנשאר בכל פרט נפש בעת שישן קוסטא דחיותא שממנה נתעורר ומקיץ משנתו כך יש בכל פרט נפש קוסטא דחיותא שיתעורר ממנה בתחיית המתים וזאת הקוסטא דחיותא נקרא נמי בזוה"ק הבלא דגרמי וכמו שהוא בהפרט כך הוא נמי בהכלל והקוסטא דחיותא מהכלל ישראל הוא אליהו הנביא שהוא חי וקים לעולם ואצלו היו ביותר כל עבודות החזקות עד שהראה בעוצם עבודתו מפורש ה' הוא האלהים שהשי"ת נמצא בכל הלבושים אפילו הרחוקים מאד כי אלהים מורה על כל הלבושים גם הרחוקים מאד כדאי' בזוה"ק (בחוקותי) אפי' ע"ז נמי בשמא דאלהים אקרי ואליהו הנביא הראה מפורש שאין שום כח אחר בעולם מבלעדי כחו ית' וכדכתיב ובכל מקום מוקטר מוגש לשמי ומנחה טהורה ולזה היה בכחו גם להקריב בחוץ אף בשעת איסור במות וכמו שנאמר שם ובדברך עשיתי את כל הדברים האלה
records.targetEnglish: Elijah is the “vapor of the bones” of all Israel. Just as in each individual soul, during sleep, a small measure of life remains from which the person awakens and rises, so in each soul a measure of life remains from which it will awaken at the resurrection of the dead. This measure is also called in the Zohar the “vapor of the bones.” As with the individual, so with the collective: the enduring measure of life of all Israel is Elijah the prophet, who lives and endures forever. He possessed especially intense acts of service, until through their strength he showed explicitly that “YHVH is God”: God is present in all the garments, even those exceedingly distant. Elohim signifies all the garments, including the most distant, as the Zohar says that even idolatry is called by the name elohim. Elijah showed expressly that no other power exists in the world apart from His power, as it is written, “In every place incense is offered to My name, and a pure offering.” Therefore he had the power to offer outside even when private altars were forbidden, as he said, “By Your word I have done all these things.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains why Elijah is associated with renewed life: he represents the abiding point of life of the whole people, analogous to the point from which an individual awakens. Its Mount Carmel interpretation also preserves “By Your word,” linking the disclosure to Elijah’s commanded service. This gives an account of the life that repentance can awaken beneath an apparently dead state.

records.originHebrew: רַק הָעִנְיָן הוּא: שֶׁבְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר יֵשׁ חֲנֻכָּה זוֹ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹשֶׂה לוֹ דִּירָה בְּלֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנַּעֲשֶׂה מִשְׁכָּן לַשְּׁכִינָה, וְעַל זֶה עוֹשִׂין חֲנֻכָּה בְּכָל יוֹם עַל חֲנֻכַּת הַשְׁרָאַת הַשְּׁכִינָה בְּלֵב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְנִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַכֹּהֲנִים הַחַשְׁמוֹנָאִים שֶׁהֵם פָּעֲלוּ זֹאת שֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בְּלֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל. וְזֶה הַנֵּר חֲנֻכָּה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּבְיָכוֹל מַדְלִיק, שֶׁמֵּאִיר בְּלֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּמְקַיֵּם מִצְוַת זְקֵנִים (כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר מַאֲמָר ב׳);
records.originEnglish: The matter is that in every generation this dedication occurs: God makes a dwelling for Himself in Israel’s heart, which becomes a sanctuary for the Divine Presence. A dedication is therefore made every day for the new resting of the Presence in the hearts of Israel. It is named for the Hasmonean priests, who brought about the revelation of Oral Torah’s light in Israel’s heart. This is the Chanukah lamp that God Himself, as it were, lights: He illuminates Israel’s heart and fulfills the elders’ commandment, as explained in ois 2.
records.themeTitle: The renewed sanctuary is built through Torah in the heart
records.themeSummary: The ois reads the present-tense dedication as a continuing event: the light of Oral Torah makes the heart a dwelling for the Divine Presence. The related passages explain the human work through which this dwelling is formed.
records.targetHebrew: ורש"י פירוש (בפ"א דאבות) עמ"ש וקנה לך חבר י"א ספרים כו' ואין המכוון שיקנה ה' חומשי תורה כי התורה שבכתב היה מספיק רק קודם הקלקול כמ"ש (נדרים כב :) אלמלא חטאו ישראל לא ניתן להם אלא ה' חומשי תורה וכו' אבל אחר הקלקול דצריך לתקן הרב כעס הוא דייקא על ידי הרוב חכמה שהוא התורה שבעל פה. ועל זה מרמז כל איש אשר ידבנו לבו דיתרע ביה קב"ה היינו החכמים שבכל דור. וצריך לקנות ספרי התנאים וגם כל הצדיקים שבכל דור הידועים לרודפי צדק מבקשי ה' וחברו ספרים בחידושי תורה שהם דברי אלהים חיים מהם תקחו את תרומתי מהם או מפי כתבם מהספרי קודש שיצא מפיהם שמהם תלמדו לאהבה וליראה את ה' ולזכות להשראת שכינה בתחתונים כנ"ל:
records.targetEnglish: Rashi explains in the first chapter of Avot, concerning “Acquire a companion for yourself,” that some say this means books. The intention is not that one should buy the Five Books of Torah, for Written Torah was sufficient only before the damage, as the Sages said: had Israel not sinned, only the Five Books of Torah would have been given to them. After the damage, however, the abundant anger must specifically be repaired through abundant wisdom, which is Oral Torah. This is hinted at in “every man whose heart moves him”—one whom God desires—meaning the sages of each generation. One must acquire the books of the tannaim and also those of the righteous of every generation, known to those who pursue righteousness and seek God, who composed books of new Torah teachings that are the words of the living God. “From them take My offering”: from them, or from their writing, the holy books issuing from their mouths, learn to love and fear God and to attain the resting of the Divine Presence below.
records.explanation: Terumah identifies how the continuing sanctuary is built: the developing Oral Torah addresses the damaged heart through added wisdom, love, and awe. Learning from the sages’ living teaching and writings therefore has a concrete role in the daily dedication described in Chanukah. This is more than a symbolic resemblance between a book and a building.

records.themeSummary: The ois reads the present-tense dedication as a continuing event: the light of Oral Torah makes the heart a dwelling for the Divine Presence. The related passages explain the human work through which this dwelling is formed.
records.targetHebrew: והענין הוא, כי כן הציב השי"ת שהתקשרות אורו של השי"ת עם הבריאה יהיה ע"י תפיסת אדם, ולזאת הוכרחו כל הדברים שבעולם הזה להיות ע"י צמצומים וגבולים אשר האדם יש לו בהם תפיסה והשגה. ולזאת כל המצות שבתורה הם נכנסים תחת גבולים של עולם שנה נפש. דהיינו במקום ובזמן ובנפש. ומחמת שהם נגבלים בגבול של עוה"ז, יש לו לאדם בהם השגה וידיעה, וכמו שאיתא בש"ס (מגילה ו:) יגעת ומצאת, וכדאיתא במדרש הוי יגע ואכול, וכמו שכתיב (שמות כ״ה:ח׳) ועשו לי מקדש ושכנתי בתוכם, היינו שישראל מפנה מקום בלבו להשראת השכינה, וכל מה שאדם מפנה מקום יותר שישרה בו אור שכינתו כן שורה בו אורו ית' יותר. כי בגבולים ההם יוכל אדם להתיגע בהם ולהכניסם בתפיסתו והשגתו, יען כי הם בגבול ותכלית וגם האדם הוא בגבול ותכלית. ומצד זה היה ראוי שגם השכר אשר ד' יעד לברואיו חלף עבודתם יהיה ג"כ מוגדר ומוגבל, למען יתאם אל הפעולה שהוא בגבול. אבל באמת השכר של השי"ת, שהשי"ת נותן לישראל חלף עבודתם, אינו בגבול ותכלית, מאחר שהוא נותן לאדם מאתו ית' שהוא אין סוף ובלי גבול ובלי תכלית, ממילא שכרו ג"כ בלי גבול ותכלית.
records.targetEnglish: God established that the bond of His light with creation should occur through human understanding. Everything in this world therefore had to come through contractions and limits within which a person can grasp and understand. All the Torah’s mitzvot enter the limits of world, year, and soul—that is, place, time, and person. Because they are bounded within this world, a person can grasp and know them: “You labored and found,” and “Labor and eat.” Thus, “Make Me a sanctuary, and I shall dwell among them”: Israel clears a place in the heart for the Divine Presence. The more space a person clears for its light, the more His light rests there. A person can labor within these limits and bring them into his understanding, because they are finite and the person too is finite. Accordingly, the reward God promised His creatures for their service should seemingly also be bounded, matching the bounded action. In truth, however, the reward God gives Israel for their service is not bounded or finite. Since He gives the person from Himself, the Infinite, without limit or end, His reward too has no limit or end.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains how a limited human heart can become a dwelling for divine light. Concrete, bounded mitzvot give the person a place to work and clear room, while the light received is a gift beyond the measure of that work. This gives substance to the Chanukah discourse’s daily inner dedication without treating a passing feeling as an already completed sanctuary.

records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁחָשַׁב מִילֵּי דַּחֲסִידוּת, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי כֵן זָכוּ לַאֲרִיכוּת יָמִים. וּלְפִי הָאָמוּר הוּא מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב: "חֲסִידוּת מְבִיאָה לִידֵי רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ לִתְחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים", דִּכְתִיב: "וְנָתַתִּי רוּחִי בָכֶם וִחְיִיתֶם" כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי, וְהַיְנוּ דְּעַל יְדֵי הַחֲסִידוּת זוֹכֶה לְחַיִּים. וּכְתִיב: "וְנָתַתִּי רוּחִי בָכֶם", "רוּחִי" דַּוְקָא, וְהַיְנוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁחִשֵּׁב בַּפָּסוּק: "וְנָחָה וְגוֹמֵר רוּחַ הַשֵּׁם וְגוֹמֵר רוּחַ דַּעַת וְיִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם", וְהַיְנוּ כְּשֶׁיִּזְכֶּה לִבְחִינַת הַדַּעַת, וּכְעֵין מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אָז תָּבִין יִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם וְדַעַת אֱלֹהִים תִּמְצָא", וְהוּא כְּשֶׁנִּכְנָס הַיִּרְאָה לְמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב שֶׁעַל זֶה מוֹרֶה "בִּינָה לִבָּא", שֶׁנִּכְנָס הַיִּרְאָה לִבְחִינַת נְקֻדָּה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, אָז זוֹכֶה לִבְחִינַת הַדַּעַת שֶׁהוּא פְּנִימִיּוּת הַכֶּתֶר כַּיָּדוּעַ. וְ"רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ", כְּלוֹמַר רוּחַ מֵהַהוּא קֹדֶשׁ דִּלְעֵילָא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג׳ ס״א עַמּוּד א׳), וְהַיְנוּ חָכְמָה עִלָּאָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁמְּקַבֵּל מֵאוֹר הַגָּנוּז, מִקּוּצָא דְּיוֹ"ד דִּלְעֵילָא דִּרְמִיזָא לְכֶתֶר עֶלְיוֹן כַּיָּדוּעַ; וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְנָתַתִּי רוּחִי בָכֶם וִחְיִיתֶם", דְּעַל יְדֵי כֵן זוֹכֶה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם, שֶׁכֵּן תְּחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים עַל יְדֵי נְהִירוּ דְּאוֹר הַגָּנוּז.
records.originEnglish: This is why the Sages counted acts of piety: through them they merited length of days. In light of what was said, this is “Piety brings to the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit to the resurrection of the dead,” as the Jerusalem Talmud cites, “I shall place My spirit within you, and you shall live.” Through piety one attains life. It says specifically “My spirit,” like the verse enumerating “the spirit of the Lord ... the spirit of knowledge and fear of the Lord.” This is the attainment of inward knowledge: “Then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find knowledge of God.” When awe enters the heart’s depths—“understanding is the heart”—and reaches its inward point, one attains knowledge, the inner aspect of Keter. “The Holy Spirit” means a spirit from that higher holiness, namely the higher wisdom receiving from the hidden light, from the upper point of the yod that alludes to the supreme Keter. Thus, “I shall place My spirit within you, and you shall live”: through this one attains eternal life, for resurrection comes through the illumination of the hidden light.
records.themeTitle: Prepared piety makes inspiration an enduring acquisition
records.themeSummary: The ois connects the extra devotion called piety to an inward knowledge, the Holy Spirit, and life. Its opening distinguishes this from a simple claim that every ordinary mitzvah earns longer earthly life.
records.targetHebrew: יש אשר בא מצד הכנת אדם, שאדם מכין עצמו ומגדיר עצמו בשביל רצון השי"ת ועי"ז בא לידי רוח הקודש. כמו שאיתא במדרש (רבה שיר א) זריזות מביאה לידי נקיות וכו' חסידות מביאה לידי רוח הקודש, והיינו שע"י שהאדם מכין עצמו בכל אלו ההכנות שמחשב המדרש, בא לידי רוח הקודש. וזה הרוח הקודש נקרא נבואה שנצרכה לדורות, כי מאחר שבא ע"י הכנת אדם הוא נשאר בקביעות אצל כל העולם.
records.targetEnglish: There is a Holy Spirit that comes through human preparation: a person prepares and sets boundaries for himself for the sake of God’s will, and through this attains the Holy Spirit. Thus the Midrash says, “Zeal brings to cleanliness ... piety brings to the Holy Spirit.” Through preparing himself with all the preparations the Midrash enumerates, he attains the Holy Spirit. This Holy Spirit is called prophecy needed for the generations, for since it came through human preparation, it remains established for the whole world.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why the preparation leading through piety matters: it makes the received illumination enduring. His full paragraph distinguishes this from a temporary inspiration bestowed without that preparation. This illuminates the lasting acquisition in Chanukah’s piety–spirit–life progression; it does not supply an independent promise of a particular number of earthly years.

records.originHebrew: וְאִיתָא (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ב׳): "'וְחֹשֶׁךְ' זֶה יָוָן וְכוּלֵיהּ", וְכֵיוָן דִּכְתִיב אַחַר כָּךְ "יְהִי אוֹר", וְהַיְנוּ דְּיִהְיֶה נְהוֹרָא הַהוּא דְּנָפַק מִגּוֹ חֲשׁוֹכָא, מוֹרֶה שֶׁהָאוֹר שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה עַל יְדֵי הַחֹשֶׁךְ שֶׁהוּא יָוָן הוּא מֵהָאוֹר הָרִאשׁוֹן. וְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק א׳ ר״ג עַמּוּד ב׳): "'וְזָרְחָה לָכֶם וְגוֹמֵר שֶׁמֶשׁ וְגוֹמֵר' הַהוּא שִׁמְשָׁא דִּגְנִיז קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא מִיּוֹמָא דְּאִתְבְּרֵי עָלְמָא וְכוּלֵיהּ"; וְלִכְאוֹרָה אֵינוֹ מוּבָן, דְּהָא הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ הוּא בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה? אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת הוּא שֶׁמִּתְּחִלָּה נִבְרָא אוֹר הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ שִׁבְעָתַיִם כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד, וְאִם לֹא הָיָה הַפְּגָם הָיָה נִשְׁאָר כֵּן; רַק אַחַר הַקִּלְקוּל נִגְנַז אוֹר הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ. וַחֲנֻכַּת עוֹלָם הַבָּא יִהְיֶה בְּאוֹר, כְּמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְהָיָה אוֹר הַלְּבָנָה וְגוֹמֵר וְאוֹר הַחַמָּה יִהְיֶה שִׁבְעָתַיִם וְגוֹמֵר" (וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּפְּסִיקְתָא פָּרָשָׁה ב׳), וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה אוֹר הָרִאשׁוֹן, וְזֶה יִהְיֶה עַל יְדֵי מָשִׁיחַ.
records.originEnglish: Bereishit Rabbah says, “‘And darkness’ is Greece.” Since afterward it says, “Let there be light,” this is the light that comes out of darkness. It shows that the light produced through the darkness of Greece belongs to the first light. The Zohar says concerning “A sun shall shine for you” that it is the sun God concealed from the day the world was created. This seems difficult, for the sun exists in this world! In truth the sun’s light was originally created sevenfold, as it will be in the future; had there been no damage, it would have remained so. Only after the damage was the sun’s light concealed. The dedication of the world to come will be through light: “The light of the moon shall be ... and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold.” The first light will be revealed, and this will occur through the Messiah.
records.themeTitle: Light won through concealment reconnects with the first light
records.themeSummary: The ois identifies the light after Greek darkness with the first light concealed after the damage. Its future restoration is thus a recovery of a deeper source through the later work of repair.
records.targetHebrew: וּבֶאֱמֶת אִם אָדָם בּוֹקֵעַ אֶת כָּל מִינֵי מַסָכִים וּמַגִּיעַ לַמַּאֲמָר הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁנִּקְרָא "יְהִי אוֹר", אָז נוֹתֵן לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חֵלֶק גַּם בְּמַאֲמַר "בְּרֵאשִׁית", שֶׁאִיתָא בַּשַּׁ"ס (מְגִלָּה כ"א ע"ב): "בְּרֵאשִׁית נַמֵּי מַאֲמָר הוּא". וְגַם בְּזֶה הַמַּאֲמָר נוֹתֵן לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חֵלֶק לָאָדָם, שֶׁעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל מַגִּיעַ גַּם לְזֶה הַמַּאֲמָר, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַרְאֶה לָאָדָם שֶׁכָּל עִנְיַן הִתְלַבְּשׁוּת הַבְּרִיאָה שֶׁהִצִּיב הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּזֶה הָעוֹלָם, מֵחֲמַת שֶׁחָפֵץ לְהֵיטִיב לִבְרִיּוֹתָיו, וְרָצָה שֶׁתִּהְיֶה נִקְרָא "יְגִיעַ כַּפּוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם", עַל כֵּן הִצִּיב הִתְלַבְּשׁוּת הַזֶּה. אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת מְקוֹמָם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא גַּם בְּמַאֲמַר בְּרֵאשִׁית הַנִּקְרָא "בְּרֵאשִׁית נַמֵּי מַאֲמָר הוּא":
records.targetEnglish: If a person breaks through all kinds of screens and reaches the first utterance called “Let there be light,” God then gives him a share even in the utterance “Bereshit,” as the Talmud says, “Bereshit too is an utterance.” In this utterance too God gives the person a share: Israel’s service reaches even this utterance. God shows the person that the entire clothing of creation that He established in this world came because He desired to benefit His creatures and wished it to be called “the labor of the person’s hands.” He therefore established this clothing. In truth, however, Israel’s place is also in the utterance Bereshit, called “Bereshit too is an utterance.”
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why light reached through later service can belong to the primordial source. Breaking through concealment does not merely restore a visible lamp; God gives the person a share in the source that preceded the concealment. This illuminates Chanukah’s identification of the later recovered light with the first light, without claiming that Tiferet is describing the Greek persecution itself.

records.originHebrew: וְכֵן בְּמוֹצָאֵי יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים אוֹמְרִים שֶׁבַע פְּעָמִים: "יהו"ה הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים", שֶׁאָז אַחַר שֶׁעָשׂוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל תְּשׁוּבָה וְנִתְגַּלָּה תַּרְעָא דְּחֵירוּ, בִּינָה, עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי, מַזְכִּירִין שֶׁבַע פְּעָמִים יִחוּד זֶה, וּמִסְפַּר שֶׁבַע הוּא מִסְפָּר הַשָּׁלֵם כַּיָּדוּעַ. וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אָז תָּבִין וְגוֹמֵר וְדעַת אֱלֹהִים תִּמְצָא", שֶׁזּוֹכִין לִבְחִינַת הַדַּעַת, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכִין לְיִחוּד בְּאֹרַח פְּרָט, וּכְמַה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְיָדַעְתָּ הַיּוֹם". וּבְכָל שָׁנָה בַּחֲנֻכָּה הַזְּמַן שֶׁיּוּכַל כָּל אָדָם לִזְכּוֹת לְתַקֵּן מַעֲשָׂיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ נֶחְשָׁבִין כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, שֶׁאִם יִפְתַּח פֶּתַח אֶחָד שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה כְּחֻדָּהּ שֶׁל מַחַט בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִצִּדּוֹ, הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מוּכָן לְעָזְרוֹ שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה תְּשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵמָה הַמְהַפֵּךְ זְדוֹנוֹת לִזְכֻיּוֹת.
records.originEnglish: At the close of Yom Kippur we likewise say seven times, “YHVH is God.” After Israel has repented and the gate of freedom—Binah, the world to come—has been revealed, this unity is mentioned seven times; seven is the number of completeness. This follows “Then you will understand ... and find knowledge of God”: one attains the inward knowledge through which this particular unity is attained, as in “Know today.” Every year Chanukah is a time when anyone can merit to repair his deeds so that they are reckoned as merits. If he opens one opening of repentance, like the point of a needle, through an awakening from his side, God is ready to help him attain the full repentance that turns deliberate sins into merits.

records.targetHebrew: וּתְשׁוּבָה אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּרֶגַע אֶחָד כִּדְמוּכָח בְּפֶרֶק ב דְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מט:), וְאָנוּ מְבַקְּשִׁים "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ וְגוֹמֵר", רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צוֹוֵחַ "שׁוּבוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה סוֹף אֵיכָה), וּמִסְּתָמָא בְּדוֹר שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ חַיָּיב עַל כָּרְחֲךָ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אָז "דִּידַן נָצַח", וּכְשֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִרְצֶה, הֲרֵי בְּרֶגַע אֶחָד יִכְלוּ כָּל הַקּוֹצִים הַסּוֹבְבִים וְיִהְיֶה הַכֹּל כִּרְצוֹנוֹ, וְיִתְגַּלֶּה שֶׁגַּם מַה שֶּׁקּוֹדֶם הָיָה הַכֹּל לְצוֹרֶךְ:
records.targetEnglish: Repentance can occur in a single moment, as is evident in the second chapter of Kiddushin. We ask, “Bring us back,” while God cries, “Return,” as the Midrash at the end of Lamentations says. Presumably, in a generation entirely guilty, “our side will prevail.” When God desires, in one moment all the surrounding thorns will be consumed, everything will be according to His will, and it will be revealed that all that preceded was also needed.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains why a deeply damaged condition does not make a present beginning impossible: repentance can start in a moment, and the exchange between “Bring us back” and “Return” keeps both divine help and the person’s response in view. Its full paragraph distinguishes the soul from the surrounding thorns. This strengthens Chanukah’s invitation to open the small beginning without declaring the whole repair already accomplished.

records.targetHebrew: ה' הוא האלהים. איתא בכתבי האר"י הק' ז"ל אשר לפי הנראה היה צריך לומר אלהים הוא ה' כי מי נתלה במי הוי אומר הקטן נתלה בגדול אכן הענין הוא כי רק בתפיסה הנמוכה של אדם שאינו יכול לצייר דבר קטן בלתי שיצייר אותה בדבר גדול שייך אצלו לומר מי נתלה במי וכו' אבל מצד השי"ת אין שייך לומר שתולה דבר בזולתה לזה נאמר שפיר ה' הוא האלהים היינו כי השם הויה מורה על הארה מפורשת. והשם אלהים מורה על התלבשות האור אשר מזה ההתלבשות נסתעפו כל הדינים היינו לבושים רחוקים כל כך שאין עוד בהם שום הכרה באורו ית' לזה נאמר ה' הוא האלהים ואלו ב' השמות ביחד מורה על שם מלא כדאיתא בזוה"ק (משפטים קיג) ושם מלא היינו שיש הכרה מפורשת איך שאור רצונו ית' הוא מלא בכל הלבושים אף בהרחוקים מאד וכמו שמצינו גבי אליהו הנביא לאחר שהקריב בחוץ והראה אור כבודו ית' אף בכל הלבושים רחוקים שמבחוץ אמר ה' הוא האלהים וכן אחר כל עבודות של יוה"כ שמנהיר אורו ית' אז אף בכל הלבושים שמבחוץ אומרים בו ה' הוא האלהים להורות שניכר אורו ית' אף דרך כמה לבושים כדכתיב וימלא כבוד ה' את כל הארץ:
records.targetEnglish: “YHVH is God.” The writings of the holy Ari observe that it should seemingly say “Elohim is YHVH,” since the smaller is related to the greater. But this principle applies only within a person’s limited understanding, which cannot picture a small thing without picturing it through a large thing. From God’s side, it is inappropriate to speak of one thing depending upon another. Thus “YHVH is Elohim” is correct. The name YHVH signifies explicit illumination, while Elohim signifies the light’s clothing, from which all judgments branch forth: garments so distant that His light is no longer recognized within them. Therefore it says “YHVH is Elohim.” The two names together signify the full name: an explicit recognition that the light of His will fills every garment, even the very distant ones. Thus Elijah, after offering outside and showing the light of His glory even in the distant outer garments, said “YHVH is Elohim.” Likewise, after all the service of Yom Kippur, when His light shines even in the outer garments, we say “YHVH is Elohim,” indicating that His light is recognized through the many garments: “The glory of the Lord shall fill the whole earth.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the declaration’s order and the meaning of its two names. The unity acknowledged after the day’s service reaches even the outer garments that had concealed the light. This clarifies why Chanukah connects completed repentance with Yom Kippur’s particular declaration, while the origin itself still calls for a person’s initial opening.

records.originHebrew: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ סְעוּדָה הִתְחִילוּ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה וּבְדִבְרֵי תֻּשְׁבָּחוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּגְּמָרָא (שָׁם י״ב עַמּוּד ב׳); וְאָז נִגְלוּ מַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב, שֶׁבִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים אָדָם נִכָּר: בְּכוֹסוֹ וְכוּלֵיהּ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב עֵירוּבִין ס״ה עַמּוּד ב׳); וְנִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל בֶּאֱמֶת קְדוֹשִׁים בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ;
records.originEnglish: By contrast, Israel at that meal began with words of Torah and words of praise, as the Talmud says. Then the depths of the heart were revealed, for a person is recognized through three things: his cup, and so forth. It became clear that Israel is truly holy at the root.
records.themeTitle: The cup reveals what has been established in the heart
records.themeSummary: In explaining Mordekhai’s place in the deliverance, the ois contrasts an outward appearance of refinement with the inner character disclosed at the feast. The criterion is the Torah and praise that actually emerge.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה הָעִנְיָן בְּנֹחַ גַּם כֵּן: אַחַר שֶׁהוּתַּר לוֹ הַבָּשָׂר כְּדֵי שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַבָּשָׂר יִזְכֶּה לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב וּלְשַׂמְּחוֹ, הָיָה נֹחַ סָבוּר שֶׁאַף הַיַּיִן נִצְרָךְ לוֹ לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב וְלִזְכּוֹת לְשִׂמְחָה, וְאֵין רְאָיָה מֵאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַקִּלְקוּל; וְזֶה הָיָה טַעֲמוֹ שֶׁנָּטַע כֶּרֶם. אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת, הַיַּיִן הַמְיַישֵּׁר הַלֵּב הוּא רַק יַיִן דְּקִדּוּשׁ שֶׁהוּא יַיִן מִצְוָה, אוֹ מִי שֶׁנִּצְרָךְ לוֹ הַיַּיִן לְיִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת לְתוֹרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג, קכד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): "חַכִּימִין דְּדַמְיָין לְשַׁבַּתּוֹת וְכוּלֵי", וְכָל אֲכִילָתָן בִּקְדוּשָׁה, כַּאֲכִילַת שַׁבָּתוֹת וְיוֹם טוֹב שֶׁכָּל אֲכִילָתָן לְקִיּוּם הַחַיִּים לְתוֹרָה; וְלָהֶם נִצְרָךְ הַיַּיִן כְּמוֹ בְּשַׁבָּת שֶׁאָדָם קוֹבֵעַ סְעוּדָתוֹ עַל הַיַּיִן.
records.targetEnglish: This was also the matter with Noah. After meat had been permitted to him so that through it he could attain an upright and joyful heart, Noah thought that wine too was needed to straighten the heart and attain joy, and that Adam before the damage furnished no proof to the contrary. This was his reason for planting a vineyard. In truth, however, the wine that straightens the heart is specifically the wine of kiddush, which is the wine of a mitzvah, or wine for someone who needs it for settled understanding in Torah. Thus the Zohar speaks of sages who resemble Shabbat: all their eating is holy, like the eating of Shabbat and festivals, all directed toward sustaining life for Torah. They need wine as on Shabbat, when a person establishes his meal over wine.
records.explanation: Lech Lecha distinguishes the conditions under which wine serves an upright heart from Noah’s unsuccessful inference that it would do so automatically. This clarifies the Torah and praise disclosed in Chanukah’s feast comparison. The record preserves the mitzvah or settled-Torah purpose; it does not turn the passage into a blanket recommendation to drink.

records.targetHebrew: וּלְזֶה יָבֹא הָאָדָם בַּעֲבוֹדָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבוֹד אֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי שֶׁיַּכְנִיס אֶת עַצְמוֹ בִּפְעֻלּוֹת וְעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִיכָּר הָאָדָם מַה הוּא. שֶׁכֵּן אִיתָא בַּשַּׁ"ס (עֵירוּבִין סה עַמּוּד ב): "בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְבָרִים אָדָם נִיכָּר: בְּכוֹסוֹ, בְּכִיסוֹ וּבְכַעֲסוֹ", וְאֵינוֹ נוֹתֵן סִימָן בָּאָדָם לְהַכִּיר אוֹתוֹ בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁעוֹמֵד בְּבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת מְלוּבָּשׁ בְּטַלִּית שֶׁל מִצְוָה וּמְעוּטָּר בִּתְפִלִּין, מַשְׁמָע שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה מִזֶּה; אָכֵן עִיקַּר הַהַכָּרָה הוּא בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁמַּכְנִיס אֶת עַצְמוֹ בְּהַסְתָּרוֹת בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, בְּעִסְקוֹ עִם הַבְּרִיּוֹת בַּשְּׁוָוקִים וּבָרְחוֹבוֹת, אָז יְכוֹלִים לְהַכִּיר הַיְּקָרוּת שֶׁבָּאָדָם מַה הוּא בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: A person reaches this through his service, serving God by entering the actions and affairs of this world. Through this it becomes recognizable what the person is. The Talmud says, “A person is recognized through three things: his cup, his purse, and his anger.” It does not give a sign by which to recognize him when he stands in the synagogue clothed in a mitzvah’s tallit and crowned with tefillin; this implies that such a sight supplies no proof. The principal recognition occurs when he enters the concealments of worldly affairs, dealing with people in markets and streets. Then the precious quality within the person, what lies in the depths of his heart, can be recognized.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains why the cup is evidence of something not established by a dignified religious appearance alone. Ordinary conduct brings inward qualities into action under concealment. This illuminates Chanukah’s distinction between an attractive exterior and the Torah-filled response actually disclosed at the feast. The preceding paragraph requires continued work and prayer to repair the root; the test of conduct is not a claim of automatic perfection.

records.originHebrew: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן נֵס חֲנֻכָּה שֶׁהָיָה בְּחִינַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "תִּזַּל כַּטַּל אִמְרָתִי", שֶׁאֵין נִכָּר יְרִידַת הַטַּל מִלְּמַעְלָה, רַק מְבִינִים כְּשֶׁרוֹאִין הָאָרֶץ לַחָה שֶׁיָּרַד הַטַּל; וְכֵן תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה נִדְמֶה לַחֲכָמִים שֶׁהֵם הַמְחַדְּשִׁים, וּבֶאֱמֶת הֵם דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים: "דְּבָרַי אֲשֶׁר שַׂמְתִּי בְּפִיךָ"; וְכֵן נֵס חֲנֻכָּה שֶׁהָיָה עַל יְדֵי מִלְחָמָה, רַק שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת הָיָה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁנָּתַן בְּלִבָּם אֹמֶץ וְחִזּוּק לַעֲמֹד בִּמְתֵי מְעַט נֶגֶד עַם רָב, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת הָיָה מִצִּדָּם; וְאַחַר כָּךְ נָתַן לָהֶם כֹּחַ וּמָסַר גִּבּוֹרִים בְּיַד חַלָּשִׁים וְרַבִּים בְּיַד מְעַטִּים, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא הָיָה הַנֵּס מְפֹרָשׁ לְעֵין כֹּל; וּבִפְרָט נֵס הַשֶּׁמֶן שֶׁהָיָה נִסְתָּר בְּוַדַּאי, וְלֹא נִתַּן לִכָּתֵב, שֶׁהָיָה בְּחִינַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה; וְנֵס חֲנֻכָּה הָיָה בֶּאֱמֶת סוֹף כָּל הַנִּסִּים.
records.originEnglish: The Chanukah miracle, by contrast, was an aspect of Oral Torah, of which we have explained “Let my saying flow like dew.” Dew’s descent from above is not visible; only when the earth is seen to be damp does one understand that dew descended. Likewise, it seems to the sages that they are the ones discovering Oral Torah’s new teachings, while in truth they are the words of the living God: “My words that I have placed in your mouth.” So too the Chanukah miracle came through war. In truth God gave them courage and strength to stand, a small number against a great people, yet the awakening came from their side. He then gave them strength, delivering the mighty into weak hands and the many into few hands. Nevertheless the miracle was not explicit before everyone’s eyes. Particularly the miracle of the oil was certainly concealed, and it was not given to be written, for it belonged to Oral Torah. The Chanukah miracle was in truth the last of all the miracles.
records.themeTitle: The new teaching is received through the sage’s understanding
records.themeSummary: The ois compares Oral Torah to dew because its divine source is not apparent in the act of human discovery. The war and the oil are read within that same mode of concealed divine assistance.
records.targetHebrew: ואי' מהאר"י הק' ז"ל שרע"ק היה שורש תושבע"פ והוא בחי' מלכות פה תושבע"פ קרינן לה וע"ז נא' תזל כטל אמרתי שאף שתושבע"פ ג"כ דברי אלהים חיים מ"מ החכם המחדש נראה לו בשעת מעשה שמחדש מעצמו וכמו טל שאינו נראה שיורד מן השמים רק כשרואין שהארץ לחה יודעין שירד טל. והרמב"ן ז"ל (ב"ב י"ב.) כתב שהוא ע"י רוה"ק מה שמכוין מדעתו לדברי אלהים חיים וכמו שא' ולאו טעמא יהיב וזה נקרא כתרה של תורה וכמו שא' (מגילה כ"ח:) במי ששונה הלכות כתרה של תורה וזה הי' חלק רע"ק:
records.targetEnglish: The holy Ari teaches that Rabbi Akiva was the root of Oral Torah. This is Malchut: “the mouth, which we call Oral Torah.” Concerning it, “Let my saying flow like dew” is said. Although Oral Torah too is the words of the living God, at the moment of discovery it appears to the sage that he is discovering it himself, like dew whose descent from Heaven is not seen; only when the earth is seen to be damp is it known that dew descended. The Ramban writes that this occurs through the Holy Spirit: by his own understanding he arrives at the words of the living God, as the Talmud asks, “Does he not give a reason?” This is called the crown of Torah, as the Sages say concerning someone who studies halakhot. This was Rabbi Akiva’s portion.
records.explanation: The Ki Teitzei discussion adds how the human side of this hidden reception works: the sage reasons and gives grounds for the teaching. Its setting is Moses encountering Rabbi Akiva’s developed Torah. This sharpens the dew comparison in Chanukah; the attributed inspiration operates through intelligible Torah reasoning, rather than making the mere experience of having a new idea sufficient.

records.originHebrew: וְאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁבְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר יֵשׁ נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁנִּקְרָא "חֲנִינָא", וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ וּמַכִּיר שֶׁהַכֹּל בָּא מֵחֶסֶד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁחוֹנֵן לִבְרִיּוֹתָיו. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ שֶׁהִתְפַּלֵּל בִּלְשׁוֹן "וָאֶתְחַנַּן" בִּלְשׁוֹן תַּחֲנוּנִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה; וּבַגְּמָרָא (סַנְהֶדְרִין מ״ד עַמּוּד ב׳): "'תַּחֲנוּנִים יְדַבֶּר רָשׁ' זֶה מֹשֶׁה", וְהַיְנוּ דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ הָיָה שֹׁרֶשׁ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, וּכְתִיב: "וְהַחָכְמָה מֵאַיִן תִּמָּצֵא", וְדָרְשׁוּ (סוֹטָה כ״א עַמּוּד ב׳): "אֵין דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה מִתְקַיְּמִין אֶלָּא בְּמִי שֶׁמֵּשִׂים עַצְמוֹ כְּמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ"; וְזֶה הָיָה מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ שֶׁהָיָה עָנָו מִכָּל הָאָדָם וְאָמַר: "וְנַחְנוּ מָה". וּבִשְׁבִיל נֶפֶשׁ כָּזֶה כָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ נִזּוֹנִין, וְהוּא דַּי לוֹ בְּקַב חֲרוּבִין, כֵּיוָן שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁהַכֹּל בְּחֶסֶד וּמַתְּנַת חִנָּם. וְרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא בְּדוֹרוֹ הָיָה הוּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ שֶׁהָיָה בְּחִינַת חֲנִינָא, וְעַל כֵּן הוּבָא הַמַּאֲמָר בְּתַעֲנִית עָלָיו, וְזֶה מַדְרֵגַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ.
records.originEnglish: We have explained that in every generation there is a soul called “Hanina”: one who knows and recognizes that everything comes from God’s kindness, by which He graciously gives to His creatures. So it was with Moses, who prayed in the language of supplication, “Va’etchanan.” The Talmud interprets “The poor person speaks supplications” as Moses. Moses was the root of Written Torah, and “Wisdom is found from nothingness”: Torah endures only in someone who makes himself as though he were nothing. Such was Moses, more humble than any person, who said, “What are we?” Through a soul like this the whole world is nourished, while a kav of carobs is sufficient for him, because he recognizes that everything is kindness and an unearned gift. Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa in his generation was that soul, the aspect of Hanina; that is why the statement in Taanit was brought concerning him. This is Moses’ degree.
records.themeTitle: Receiving as a gift makes room for the nourishment of others
records.themeSummary: The ois interprets the continuing announcement about Hanina through a quality present in every generation: humble recognition of the gift, joined to contentment with what actually suffices.
records.targetHebrew: דִּלְצַעוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ אָסוּר רַק בִּבְרָכָה נֶאֱמַר (תּוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים בְּחֻקֹּתַי): "אוֹכֵל קִמְעָא וּמִתְבָּרֵךְ בְּמֵעָיו" וְאִיתָא סוֹף פֶּרֶק ב׳ דִּבְרָכוֹת (דַּף י״ז עַמּוּד ב׳): "חֲנִינָא בְּנִי דַּי לוֹ בְּקַב [חֲרוּבִין מֵעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת לְעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת]" וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁדַּי לוֹ בָּזֶה וְאֵין צָרִיךְ יוֹתֵר
records.targetEnglish: For afflicting oneself is forbidden. Rather, the blessing says, “He eats a little, and it is blessed within him.” Thus, “Hanina My son is satisfied with a kav of carobs from one Shabbat eve to the next”: this is sufficient for him, and he needs no more.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek distinguishes genuine sufficiency from self-affliction. This is essential to Chanukah’s description of Hanina’s small portion: its value is that it truly suffices under blessing, not that the body is deliberately left without what it needs. The complete target paragraph expressly places this within the obligation to sustain the life entrusted to a person.

records.targetHebrew: ומחמת זאת ההתקרבות שהיה אצלו היה נמי בכחו לצמצם עצמו בכל הטובות שבעולם כדי שילכו לישראל יותר בשפע אף שבאמת ירדו כל הטובות רק בשבילו כ"ד בגמ' (שם) כל העולם ניזון בשביל חנינא בני וחנינא בני די לו בקב חרובין מע"ש וכו' וזה היה משום שהיה קרוב מאד להשי"ת והיה רואה היטב כמו שהוא באמת ה' אלהינו ה' אחד לכן היה בו נדיבות ענום כ"כ וכן באמת כל פרט נפש שיש בו גודל נדיבות להכנוסיא שלו יכול ג"כ לפעול בעדם כל הישועות אף למעלה מהטבע ולרמוז זאת מביא הגמרא (שם) כל המעשיות הנפלאים שהיו גבי רחב"ד
records.targetEnglish: Because of this closeness, he also had the power to limit himself in all the world’s benefits so that they would flow more abundantly to Israel, although in truth all the benefits descended through him: “The entire world is nourished through Hanina My son, while Hanina My son is satisfied with a kav of carobs from one Shabbat eve...” Because he was very close to God and saw clearly, as it truly is, that “The Lord our God, the Lord is one,” he possessed such immense generosity. Indeed, every individual soul possessing great generosity toward its community can effect deliverances for them, even beyond nature. To indicate this the Talmud brings all the wondrous events concerning Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the social direction of Hanina’s contentment: his nearness to God expresses itself as generosity, leaving greater abundance for others. That gives a concrete relation between the two halves of the announcement in Chanukah—the world nourished through him and his own sufficient small portion. It is not a claim that deprivation by itself produces a miracle.

records.originHebrew: אָמְנָם רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא, שֶׁהָיָה נֶפֶשׁ חֲנִינָא בְּדוֹרוֹ, שֶׁהִכִּיר שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁחוֹנֵן, לֹא הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לְמַעֲשֵׂה נִסִּים כְּלָל; שֶׁזֶּה רַק מִי שֶׁמֻּרְגָּל בַּטֶּבַע כָּמוֹנוּ, וּכְשֶׁרוֹאֶה דָּבָר הַיּוֹצֵא מֵהַטֶּבַע הוּא נֵס, כְּמוֹ אֶצְלֵנוּ שֶׁנִּרְאֶה מַה שֶּׁשֶּׁמֶן דּוֹלֵק הוּא בַּטֶּבַע, וְשֶׁיִּדְלַק חֹמֶץ הוּא נֵס; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא הִכִּיר מְפֹרָשׁ שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּמַה שֶּׁהַשֶּׁמֶן דּוֹלֵק הוּא גַּם כֵּן בְּנֵס מִמַּעֲשֵׂה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְ"הוּא יֹאמַר לַחֹמֶץ וְיִדְלַק", וְהַכֹּל אֶחָד.
records.originEnglish: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, the Hanina-soul of his generation, recognized that everything comes from God, who gives graciously. For him the category of a miraculous act did not apply. It applies to people habituated to nature, like us, who call something a miracle when they see it depart from nature. To us, oil burning seems natural and vinegar burning a miracle. Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, however, explicitly recognized that everything comes from God: oil’s burning is also a miracle wrought by Him. “He will tell vinegar to burn”—it is all one.
records.themeTitle: Habit hides the divine word sustaining ordinary nature
records.themeSummary: The ois distinguishes an ordinary observer’s categories from Rabbi Hanina’s recognition. It retains the earlier question about requesting and benefiting from miracles; his exceptional perception supplies the explanation.
records.targetHebrew: וכמו שמצינו ברחב"ד (תענית כה.) שאמר מי שאמר לשמן וידליק הוא יאמר לחומץ וידליק, ולמה הזכיר מי שאמר לשמן וידליק, רק שצריך להזכיר שכן הטביע השי"ת בטבע השמן וידליק ועל ידי זה יוכל להמשיך שיאמר לחומץ וידליק, ועל דרך ששמעתי מרה"ק זצלה"ה שאמר שמה שמצינו באלישע ויקצב עץ וישלך שמה ויצף הברזל ולמה הוצרך לקצוב עץ ולהשליך, רק שרצה להזכיר שהטביע השי"ת בעץ שיצף ע"פ המים ועל ידי זה השליך שיתן השי"ת טבע זו גם בברזל ואלישע עשה זה במעשה ורחב"ד זכר זה בפה מי שאמר לשמן וידליק כו ואצלו לא היה זה מעשה נסים דאז בודאי לא היה רוצה ליהנות ממעשה נסים (כמש"ש כד:) רק כיון שהיה ברור לנצח עיניו שאין שום טבע והרגל רק מה שהשי"ת נותן בזה הטבע והיה דומה לפניו מה ששמן דולק כמו שהיה חומץ דולק, ועל ידי שזכר בפה מי שאמר לשמן וידליק שזה רק ממאמר השי"ת על ידי זה המשיך ההשפעה לחומץ שידליק,
records.targetEnglish: Thus Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa said, “He who told oil to burn will tell vinegar to burn.” Why did he mention “He who told oil to burn”? He needed to recall that God had implanted in oil its nature to burn; through this he could draw down the command that vinegar should burn. Similarly, I heard from the holy master concerning Elisha: “He cut a piece of wood, cast it there, and the iron floated.” Why did he need to cut and cast wood? He wished to recall that God had implanted in wood the nature of floating on water, and by casting it he sought that God give this nature to iron too. Elisha did this through an act, while Rabbi Hanina recalled it with his mouth. To him this was not a miraculous act; otherwise he certainly would not have wished to benefit from it. It was clear before his eyes that there is no independent nature or habit, only the nature God gives to a thing. Oil burning was to him like vinegar burning. By verbally recalling “He who told oil to burn,” acknowledging that this occurs only through God’s utterance, he drew the flow to the vinegar so that it would burn.
records.explanation: The Pesach discussion explains the wording that Chanukah quotes. Mentioning oil is an act of recollection: the familiar property itself is grounded in a divine command, and the unusual event is approached through that recognition. The excerpt retains Rabbi Hanina’s exceptional clarity and the prohibition problem that his clarity answers; it does not generalize his conduct to an ordinary observer.

records.targetHebrew: ובאותו הסדר אין שייך כלל לומר על שינוי הטבע שהוא נס ופלא מאחר שבהארת זה הסדר ניכר מפורש לעיני כל איך שהשי"ת שופע חיים להבריאה בכל רגע ורגע שאם נפסק ח"ו השפעת החיים אפילו רגע אחת הי' נתבטל ח"ו כל קיום הויית הבריאה ואם כן איך שייך לומר על איזה שינוי שהוא נס ופלא כיון שרואים פלא כזאת בכל רגע ורגע וכמו שהי' גבי אדם הראשון מיד ביום הראשון כשנברא וכי הי' יכול אז לסבור בדעתו על דבר חדש שהי' רואה שהוא נס ופלא מאחר שהכל הי' חדש אצלו וכל מה שראו עיניו הי' לגבי' נס ופלא כשראה את הים הולך וסוער הי' לפלא אצלו. אולם אחר שהורגל כך ומהרגל נעשה טבע עד שנדמה שהטבע מחייב כך שהים ילך תמיד ואח"כ אם יראה שעמד הים מזעפו ונהפך ליבשה אזי לנס ופלא יחשב כי נשתנה הטבע. אכן כאשר פתח השי"ת בתפיסת ישראל מהסדר אמתי כמו שהוא באמת אצלו ית' שוב הכירו ישראל שפיר בתפיסתם ממש כמו אדם הראשון מיד כשנברא אשר מי שיאמר להים שילך יאמר להים שלא ילך
records.targetEnglish: Within that order (as it stands from God’s side), a change of nature cannot be called a miracle or wonder. When that order shines, everyone sees explicitly that God gives life to creation at every moment. If the flow of life ceased for even a moment, the entire existence of creation would cease. How, then, can a particular change be called a wonder, when such a wonder is seen at every moment? It was like Adam immediately on the first day of his creation. Could he consider some newly seen thing a miracle, when everything was new to him and everything his eyes saw was a wonder? Seeing the sea moving and surging was itself a wonder to him. Only afterward, when he became accustomed to it and habit became nature, did it seem that nature required the sea always to move. If he then saw the sea stand still and become dry land, he would consider it a miracle because nature had changed. But when God opened Israel’s understanding to the true order as it is with Him, they recognized it in their own understanding just as Adam did immediately after creation: He who tells the sea to move can tell it not to move.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the role of habit in the distinction Chanukah draws. The familiar event seems self-sustaining only because its constant renewal is no longer noticed. The greater disclosure is that creation receives life at every moment. This gives a precise account of Rabbi Hanina’s seeing the same divine act in oil and vinegar.

records.originHebrew: וְעַל יְדֵי הַשִּׁפְלוּת מַכִּירִין שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חוֹנֵן, כְּעִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן" אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ הָגוּן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרָכוֹת ז׳ עַמּוּד א׳). וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר שֶׁנֶּרְמַז גַּם כֵּן בְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּאֶסְתֵּר: "וַתְּהִי אֶסְתֵּר נֹשֵׂאת חֵן וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁרוֹמֵז שֶׁהִכִּירָה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּחֵן וּבְחֶסֶד, וְעַל יְדֵי כֵן: "וַתִּלְבַּשׁ אֶסְתֵּר מַלְכוּת", שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ בַּגְּמָרָא וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג׳ קס״ט עַמּוּד ב׳) שֶׁלְּבָשַׁתָּהּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְהַיְנוּ מִדַּת מַלְכוּת; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁעַל זֶה רוֹמֵז שֶׁהִיא סוֹף כָּל הַנִּסִּים שֶׁמְּכֻוָּן נֶגֶד מִדַּת מַלְכוּת. וְאִיתָא (בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה וּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא מַטּוֹת): שָׁלֹשׁ מַתָּנוֹת בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּעוֹלָם: חָכְמָה, וּגְבוּרָה, וְעֹשֶׁר וְכוּלֵיהּ; וְאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁהֵם נֶגֶד חַיֵּי, בָּנֵי וּמְזוֹנֵי: דְּתוֹרָה עִקַּר הַחַיִּים, וּכְתִיב: "הַחָכְמָה תְּחַיֶּה בְעָלֶיהָ"; וּגְבוּרָה נֶגֶד בָּנֵי, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א פֶּרֶק ח׳): "גִּבּוֹרֵי חַיִל וְגוֹמֵר וּמַרְבִּים בָּנִים וּבְנֵי בָנִים"; וְעֹשֶׁר הַיְנוּ מְזוֹנֵי (וְנִתְבָּאֵר פָּרָשַׁת וַיִּשְׁלַח מַאֲמָר ו׳); וְאִיתָא בַּמִּדְרָשׁ שָׁם: אֵימָתַי? בִּזְמַן שֶׁהֵם מַתְּנוֹת שָׁמַיִם וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁהָעִקָּר שֶׁיַּכִּירוּ כִּי הֵם מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְנָתַן לָהֶם בְּמַתְּנַת חִנָּם. וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּחָכְמָה: "אַתָּה חוֹנֵן וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְחָנֵּנוּ מֵאִתְּךָ וְכוּלֵיהּ, חוֹנֵן הַדָּעַת".
records.originEnglish: Through humility one recognizes that God gives graciously, as in “I shall favor whom I favor”—even one who is not worthy. This may also be hinted at in “Esther found favor”: she recognized that everything comes from God through favor and kindness, and through this “Esther clothed herself in royalty,” which the Talmud and Zohar interpret as her clothing herself in the Holy Spirit, the aspect of Malchut. As explained, this is why she is the end of the miracles, corresponding to Malchut. The Midrash says that God created three gifts in the world: wisdom, strength, and wealth. We have explained that these correspond to life, children, and sustenance. Torah is the essence of life—“Wisdom gives life to its owner.” Strength corresponds to children, as in the mighty warriors who increased sons and grandsons; wealth corresponds to sustenance. The Midrash asks: when are these good? When they are gifts of Heaven. The essential thing is to recognize that they come from God as an unearned gift. Thus we say concerning wisdom, “You graciously grant ... graciously grant us from Yourself ... Who graciously grants knowledge.”
records.themeTitle: Even the powers of devotion are received as a gift
records.themeSummary: The ois extends humble recognition from the rescue to wisdom, strength, and sustenance. Knowing that these are gifts allows both gratitude and continued service, without claiming that the recipient independently owns the source.
records.targetHebrew: וְהוּא ״פֶּלֶא״ — דָּבָר מֻפְלָא וְנֶעְלָם דְּלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ ״פֶּלֶא״ עַל הַנֵּס, דְּמַה פֶּלֶא הוּא לְגַבֵּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה נֵס וּ״מִי שֶׁאָמַר לַשֶּׁמֶן וְיִדְלַק, הוּא יֹאמַר לַחֹמֶץ וְיִדְלַק״ (תַּעֲנִית כ״ה עַמּוּד א׳) וְכִי דֶּרֶךְ הַטֶּבַע אֵינוֹ פֶּלֶא, אֶלָּא שֶׁכָּךְ יִסֵּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּכְשֶׁיִּרְצֶה לְשַׁנּוֹת הַטֶּבַע מִי מְעַכֵּב בְּיָדוֹ אֲבָל: ״לָא עָבֵיד קֻדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא נִיסָא לְשִׁקְרָא״ (שַׁבָּת נ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳), וְהַכֹּל בְּמִשְׁפָּט וּכְשֶׁאֵינוֹ כְּפִי הַמִּשְׁפָּט, זֶה נִקְרָא ״פֶּלֶא״: שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה נֵס לְשֶׁאֵין רָאוּי לוֹ וְדָבָר זֶה רַק עַל יְדֵי הִתְגַּלּוּת פֶּלֶא הָעֶלְיוֹן, מְקוֹם הַמֻּפְלָא דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲחִידוּ בֵּיהּ שֶׁעָלוּ בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה הַיְינוּ עֹומֶק רֵאשִׁית דְּמַחֲשָׁבָה, שֶׁהוּא הָאַיִן הַקּוֹדֵם לַיֵּשׁ שֶׁבַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה דְּהֵם זֶרַע אֱמֶת, ״אֵין אֱמֶת אֶלָּא תוֹרָה״ (בְּרָכוֹת ה׳ עַמּוּד ב׳), וּמַאן דְּאָחֵיד בְּאוֹרַיְיתָא אָחֵיד בְּכוּלָּא עַד רֵישׁ כָּל דַּרְגִּין
records.targetEnglish: This is a “wonder”—something wondrous and concealed. “Wonder” does not properly refer to the miracle itself: what wonder is it for God to perform a miracle? “He who told oil to burn will tell vinegar to burn.” Is the natural order not itself wondrous? God established it so, and when He wishes to change it, who can prevent Him? But “the Holy One does not perform a miracle for falsehood”: everything follows judgment. When it is not according to the apparent judgment, that is called a wonder—performing a miracle for someone not worthy of it. This occurs only through the revelation of the supreme wonder, the wondrous place to which Israel is bound, having arisen first in thought: the depth of the beginning of thought, the nothingness preceding the being within thought. They are the seed of truth, and “truth is Torah”; whoever is bound to Torah is bound to everything, to the head of all degrees.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz distinguishes altering nature from the deeper wonder of deliverance beyond apparent desert. It locates the latter in Israel’s prior root, while explicitly retaining divine judgment. This clarifies the grace toward the unworthy that Chanukah joins to humble recognition, rather than treating grace as a person’s entitlement.

records.originHebrew: וְעַל יְדֵי הַשִּׁפְלוּת מַכִּירִין שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חוֹנֵן, כְּעִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן" אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ הָגוּן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרָכוֹת ז׳ עַמּוּד א׳). וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר שֶׁנֶּרְמַז גַּם כֵּן בְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּאֶסְתֵּר: "וַתְּהִי אֶסְתֵּר נֹשֵׂאת חֵן וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁרוֹמֵז שֶׁהִכִּירָה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּחֵן וּבְחֶסֶד, וְעַל יְדֵי כֵן: "וַתִּלְבַּשׁ אֶסְתֵּר מַלְכוּת", שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ בַּגְּמָרָא וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג׳ קס״ט עַמּוּד ב׳) שֶׁלְּבָשַׁתָּהּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְהַיְנוּ מִדַּת מַלְכוּת; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁעַל זֶה רוֹמֵז שֶׁהִיא סוֹף כָּל הַנִּסִּים שֶׁמְּכֻוָּן נֶגֶד מִדַּת מַלְכוּת. וְאִיתָא (בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה וּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא מַטּוֹת): שָׁלֹשׁ מַתָּנוֹת בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּעוֹלָם: חָכְמָה, וּגְבוּרָה, וְעֹשֶׁר וְכוּלֵיהּ; וְאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁהֵם נֶגֶד חַיֵּי, בָּנֵי וּמְזוֹנֵי: דְּתוֹרָה עִקַּר הַחַיִּים, וּכְתִיב: "הַחָכְמָה תְּחַיֶּה בְעָלֶיהָ"; וּגְבוּרָה נֶגֶד בָּנֵי, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א פֶּרֶק ח׳): "גִּבּוֹרֵי חַיִל וְגוֹמֵר וּמַרְבִּים בָּנִים וּבְנֵי בָנִים"; וְעֹשֶׁר הַיְנוּ מְזוֹנֵי (וְנִתְבָּאֵר פָּרָשַׁת וַיִּשְׁלַח מַאֲמָר ו׳); וְאִיתָא בַּמִּדְרָשׁ שָׁם: אֵימָתַי? בִּזְמַן שֶׁהֵם מַתְּנוֹת שָׁמַיִם וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁהָעִקָּר שֶׁיַּכִּירוּ כִּי הֵם מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְנָתַן לָהֶם בְּמַתְּנַת חִנָּם. וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּחָכְמָה: "אַתָּה חוֹנֵן וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְחָנֵּנוּ מֵאִתְּךָ וְכוּלֵיהּ, חוֹנֵן הַדָּעַת".
records.originEnglish: Through humility one recognizes that God gives graciously, as in “I shall favor whom I favor”—even one who is not worthy. This may also be hinted at in “Esther found favor”: she recognized that everything comes from God through favor and kindness, and through this “Esther clothed herself in royalty,” which the Talmud and Zohar interpret as her clothing herself in the Holy Spirit, the aspect of Malchut. As explained, this is why she is the end of the miracles, corresponding to Malchut. The Midrash says that God created three gifts in the world: wisdom, strength, and wealth. We have explained that these correspond to life, children, and sustenance. Torah is the essence of life—“Wisdom gives life to its owner.” Strength corresponds to children, as in the mighty warriors who increased sons and grandsons; wealth corresponds to sustenance. The Midrash asks: when are these good? When they are gifts of Heaven. The essential thing is to recognize that they come from God as an unearned gift. Thus we say concerning wisdom, “You graciously grant ... graciously grant us from Yourself ... Who graciously grants knowledge.”

records.targetHebrew: ועל זה אמר הכתוב (ירמיהו ט׳:כ״ב) אל יתהלל חכם בחכמתו ואל יתהלל הגבור בגבורתו אל יתהלל עשיר בעשרו. וכמו שביאר בזה כבוד אזמו"ר הגה"ק זללה"ה, שהכתוב לא מיירי מדברי עוה"ז אלא, איזהו גבור הכובש את יצרו, ואיזה עשיר השמח בחלקו, היינו שישרה נפשו בו, וחכם היינו שמנהיר בלבבו אור תורה. אכן אין לו לאדם להתהלל את עצמו מזה ולקבל מזה לעצמו איזה כח ח"ו, רק כמו שמסיים הכתוב (שם) כי אם בזאת יתהלל המתהלל השכל וידוע אותי וגו'. היינו שהגבור הכובש את יצרו יכיר היטב, שזה הכח להתגבר על כל המניעות נתן לו השי"ת רק לעבודתו ית'. וכן השמח בחלקו יכיר היטב, שזה הכח מנהיר לו השי"ת. וכן החכם באור תורתו, יכיר היטב שאין זאת מצידו כלל רק שהשי"ת חנן לו בכל פעם לעבודתו ית'.
records.targetEnglish: Concerning this the verse says, “Let the wise person not boast of his wisdom, nor the mighty person of his might, nor the wealthy person of his wealth.” My holy grandfather explained that the verse is not discussing worldly matters. “Who is mighty? One who masters his inclination”; “Who is wealthy? One who rejoices in his portion,” whose soul is settled within him; and the wise person is one in whose heart Torah’s light shines. Yet a person should not boast of these attainments and take an independent power from them. Rather, the verse concludes, “Only in this should the one who boasts boast: understanding and knowing Me.” The one who masters his inclination must recognize that God gave him the power to overcome all obstacles solely for His service. One who rejoices in his portion must recognize that God illuminates this power within him. The sage, in the light of his Torah, must recognize that none of it comes independently from him: God graciously grants it to him each time for His service.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef extends the warning against self-credit to the very attainments a religious person might claim as his own: self-restraint, contentment, and Torah wisdom. That is the practical depth of Chanukah’s three gifts. Humility does not cancel their use; it identifies their purpose as continued service.

records.originHebrew: וְכֵן יוֹסֵף מֶרְכָּבָה לְמִדַּת צַדִּיק יְסוֹד עוֹלָם, "כִּי כֹל בַּשָּׁמַיִם וּבָאָרֶץ", וּמְתַרְגְּמִינַן: "דְּאָחִיד בִּשְׁמַיָּא וְאַרְעָא", שָׁמַיִם קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְהַיְנוּ גַּם כֵּן שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא. וְכֵן מִדַּת יוֹסֵף שֶׁהָיָה גִּבּוֹר הַכּוֹבֵשׁ אֶת יִצְרוֹ, וְהַיְנוּ עַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ: "לֵית לָךְ מִלָּה לְתַבְרָא יֵצֶר הָרָע אֶלָּא אוֹרַיְּתָא"; וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (סֻכָּה נ״ב עַמּוּד ב׳): "אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנֻוָּל זֶה, מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ", וּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ הַיְנוּ מְקוֹם חִדּוּשׁ הֲלָכוֹת, וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן בְּחִינַת הוֹד, דַּרְגָּא דְּאַהֲרֹן.
records.originEnglish: Joseph likewise is a vehicle for the quality of the righteous one, the foundation of the world: “For all that is in Heaven and earth,” translated as “who joins Heaven and earth.” Heaven signifies the Holy One; this too means recognizing that everything comes from Him. Joseph’s quality was also that of the mighty person who masters his inclination, through Oral Torah. As we have explained, the Zohar says of this, “Nothing breaks the evil inclination except Torah.” The Talmud likewise says, “If this repulsive one meets you, draw him into the house of study.” The house of study is the place of discovering new halakhot; this too is the aspect of Hod, Aaron’s degree.
records.themeTitle: Receiving strength from God calls for clearer chosen restraint
records.themeSummary: The ois joins Joseph’s recognition that everything comes from God to his actual mastery of the inclination. New Oral Torah supplies the strength and discernment needed for that work.
records.targetHebrew: כי חיים הוא לנו עוז ואורה. שע"י התורה נמצא הכח להכניע היצה"ר בעוז ואורה. עוז הוא בחי' התוקף להתגבר על יצה"ר המסית לדבר עבירה כאמרם ז"ל (אבות פ"ד) איזהו גבור הכובש את יצרו והוא ע"י כח התורה כאמרם ז"ל (קידושין ל':) בראתי יצה"ר בראתי תורה תבלין. ואורה הוא שע"י התורה מאירה להאדם החושך שמחשיך יצה"ר על האדם לפעמים להטעותו שהוא עושה בזה מצוה כאמרם ז"ל (חולין צ"א.) על ויאבק איש עמו שנדמה לו לת"ח שבא להטעותו בזה שנדמה לו כרבו המלמדו חכמה להועיל וע"י התורה מאירה להאדם לבל ילכד במצודתו השם חשך לאור
records.targetEnglish: For it is life to us, strength and light. Through Torah comes the power to subdue the evil inclination by strength and light. Strength is the force to overcome an inclination that urges a transgression: “Who is mighty? One who masters his inclination.” This occurs through Torah’s power: “I created the evil inclination; I created Torah as its remedy.” Light means that Torah illuminates the darkness that the inclination sometimes casts upon a person, deceiving him into thinking that he is performing a mitzvah. Thus the Sages interpret “A man wrestled with him” as the adversary appearing to him as a Torah scholar, deceiving him by appearing as his teacher who teaches beneficial wisdom. Torah illuminates the person so that he is not caught in this trap, changing darkness to light.
records.explanation: The Sukkot passage gives the study-house counsel two distinct functions. Torah strengthens resistance to a recognized wrong and also exposes a wrong disguised as a mitzvah. This explains why renewed understanding, not determination alone, belongs to Joseph’s mastery of the inclination in Chanukah.

records.themeTitle: Receiving strength from God calls for clearer chosen restraint
records.themeSummary: The ois joins Joseph’s recognition that everything comes from God to his actual mastery of the inclination. New Oral Torah supplies the strength and discernment needed for that work.

records.targetEnglish: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair said to the River Ginnai: it is true that a person possesses choice and is therefore called only “one who may accomplish.” Yet within that uncertainty of choice, I carry out His will more than you do in certainty. We possess choice; moreover, when the evil inclination is present, no one recalls the good inclination. A person could even remain without choice and say, like the creatures without choice, “The Lord is mighty on high.” Yet I do not wish to rely on the assurance that God directs me without my choice, beyond my understanding, merely saying “The Lord is mighty on high.” I continually work to fulfill His will within my own understanding and bring the Divine Presence down into my actions, so as to perform His will through my good choice. Justice therefore also requires that my uncertain act displace your certain one. In the place of my choice you have no dealings with God, whereas I continually deal with Him, illuminating through my service even a place without choice and restraining myself there too through my good choice. Joseph’s coffin alludes to this restraint. Therefore the Sages say, “The sea saw and fled”—it saw Joseph’s coffin and fled.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains why recognition of divine direction must not become reliance on passivity. Joseph’s restraint brings willing service into the very place where the inclination makes choice seem absent. This deepens the combination in Chanukah of “everything comes from God” and active mastery; the target does not itself develop the separate Oral Torah argument.

records.originEnglish: Chanukah too prepares for redemption. We have explained the Talmud’s “four craftsmen”: the Messiah son of David, the Messiah son of Joseph, Elijah, and the righteous priest. What does the righteous priest have to do with this? Shem was the first priest and taught Torah. He is called a craftsman because through Torah he built a sanctuary in the heart and soul. Elijah is the last priest, who will teach Israel all the secrets of Oral Torah before the world to come. The two Messiahs then follow: the Messiah son of Joseph will clarify “Your people are all righteous,” and the Messiah son of David will be the individual who repents, so that even one who damaged can be repaired through repentance. They are the four craftsmen of the future building, which will descend built and perfected. Elijah and the righteous priest bring Torah inward, while the Messiahs repair the foolish heart, when God will slaughter the evil inclination. So it is with Chanukah: through lighting the lamps, the light of Oral Torah shines in the heart. The miracle of oil and lamps points to wisdom and Oral Torah; it likewise prepares for the future redemption.

records.targetEnglish: In every generation there are two leaders, analogous to the Messiah son of David and the Messiah son of Joseph, especially in the footsteps of the Messiah. They correspond to the two degrees of penitents and the completely righteous, and they open these two gates anew in every generation. Every Israelite soul includes both, for both include the whole people. All Israel is named for Joseph, “the remnant of Joseph,” and for Judah, “Jews.” The latter is their principal name, since “there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin.” From Joseph they are only a remnant, since the main part was absorbed and lost in the exile of the ten tribes. That is: each person has matters in which he is righteous. As the early authorities explained concerning donkey-drivers, in one respect they are called trustworthy and in another wicked. In those matters he possesses the degree of a completely righteous person.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz brings the two future figures into the present work of each soul. A person has particular areas of uprightness and other areas needing return, and both gates must be renewed. This explains how Chanukah can prepare now for the twofold repair that its four-craftsmen conclusion places in the future.

records.targetHebrew: היינו כי בני אפרים ממהרים את הקץ טרם הזמן לזה איתא בזוה"ק דאית תרין משיחין משיח בן יוסף ומשיח בן דוד אמנם עיקר הקץ יהי' נגמר רק ע"י משיח בן דוד אכן טרם שנגמר הקץ נתעורר קודם משיח בן יוסף כי בני רחל מקדימין תמיד וממהרים את הזמן כענין שאול המלך שהי' צריך להיות טרם מלכות בית דוד כי בני' של רחל מתגברים תמיד בעבודות חזקות וממהרים את הקץ טרם החק והזמן שקצב השי"ת ומפאת זה אי אפשר שיגמור הישועה בשלימות על ידם כי אם ע"י משיח בן דוד שנמשלו לסיהרא דלית לה מגרמה כלום וממתינים את העת והזמן כפי שקצב הרצון ית' באור הנהגתו ית'
records.targetEnglish: The descendants of Ephraim hasten the end before its time. Thus the Zohar speaks of two Messiahs, the son of Joseph and the son of David, but the end is principally completed only through the son of David. Before it is completed, the son of Joseph awakens first. Rachel’s descendants always precede and hasten the time, like King Saul, who had to precede the kingship of David’s house. Rachel’s descendants exert themselves in forceful service and hasten the end before the appointed time God has fixed. Therefore the deliverance cannot be completed through them, but through the son of David, whose house is likened to the moon that has nothing of its own and waits for the time appointed by the divine will in the light of His direction.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains why the preparatory force and the final completion have different roles. Powerful service can open the way, while complete deliverance requires receiving the time God gives. This illuminates Chanukah’s sequence without treating the valuable work of Joseph’s mode as itself the finished redemption.

records.originHebrew: וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁבְּכ״ד יָמִים שֶׁבְּכִסְלֵו הָיָה הַמִּלְחָמָה וְהַנִּצּוּחַ, וְהוּא נֶגֶד כ״ד אוֹתִיּוֹת יִחוּדָא תַּתָּאָה "בָּרוּךְ שֵׁם כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ לְעוֹלָם וָעֶד", שֶׁהָיָה הַהֶאָרָה מִמִּדַּת מַלְכוּת, בְּחִינַת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁמָּסְרוּ נַפְשָׁם לִלְחֹם מְעַטִּים כְּנֶגֶד רַבִּים כְּדֵי לִשְׁמֹר מִצְוֹת הַשֵּׁם, שֶׁרָצוּ "לְהַשְׁכִּיחָם תּוֹרָתֶךָ". וְאַחַר כָּךְ בְּכ״ה בְּכִסְלֵו חָנוּ, שֶׁזָּכוּ לִנְיָחָא, וְיָכְלוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת חֲנֻכַּת הַמִּקְדָּשׁ וּלְהַדְלִיק נֵרוֹת; וְקָבְעוּ הַחֲנֻכָּה בְּיוֹם הַחֲנָיָה וְלֹא בִּימֵי הַמִּלְחָמָה שֶׁהָיָה אָז הַנֵּס, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁעִקַּר קְבִיעַת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בְּיוֹם הַחֲנָיָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁקָּבְעוּ מוֹעֵד פּוּרִים גַּם כֵּן: "כַּיָּמִים אֲשֶׁר נָחוּ בָהֶם וְגוֹמֵר".
records.originEnglish: During the twenty-four days of Kislev there was battle and victory. These correspond to the twenty-four letters of the lower unity, “Blessed is the name of the glory of His kingdom forever and ever.” The illumination came from the quality of kingship, the aspect of the community of Israel: they risked their lives, a few fighting against many, to keep God’s commandments, while the enemy sought “to make them forget Your Torah.” Afterward, on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, they encamped: they attained rest and could dedicate the Temple and light the lamps. They established Chanukah on the day of encampment, rather than during the days of battle when the miracle occurred, because the principal establishment of holiness takes place on the day of rest. Similarly, they established the festival of Purim “as the days on which they rested.”
records.themeTitle: Rest makes the attained light a settled possession
records.themeSummary: The ois distinguishes the effort of battle from the rest in which holiness can be established. Its lower and upper unities describe the relation between chosen service and the perception that emerges through it.
records.targetHebrew: [וְאֵין הַכַּוָּנָה בְּשַׁלְוָה גּוּפָנִית לְבַד וּלְהִתְעַנֵּג בַּחֲמוּדוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דְּזֶה וַדַּאי אֵינוֹ חַיִּים, וְלֹא דִּבְּרָה תּוֹרָה בַּמֵּתִים אוֹתָם שֶׁבְּחַיֵּיהֶם קְרוּיִם מֵתִים (בְּרָכוֹת י״ט עַמּוּד א׳), וּבְתָמִיד [ל״ב עַמּוּד א׳]: "מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה אָדָם וְיִחְיֶה? יָמִית אֶת עַצְמוֹ; מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה אָדָם וְיָמוּת? יְחַיֶּה אֶת עַצְמוֹ", וְאֵין נִקְרָא חַי אֶלָּא הַדָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "וְאַתֶּם הַדְּבֵקִים וְגוֹמֵר חַיִּים כֻּלְּכֶם", וְאֵין נִקְרָא חַי אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁהַחַיּוּת דָּבוּק בּוֹ וְאֵין נִפְרָד, וְעַל כָּל אֶחָד [בְּרָכוֹת י״ח עַמּוּד ב׳]: "בֶּן אִישׁ חַי" — צַדִּיקִים שֶׁבְּמִיתָתָן קְרוּיִם חַיִּים, וְזֶהוּ נִקְרָא חַי סְתָם, דְּאֵין חַיּוּת אֶלָּא הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מֵחֵי הָעוֹלָמִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם", וְזוּלַת זֶה אֵינוֹ חַיּוּת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהוּא יִתְבָּרַךְ קַיָּם לָעַד, כָּךְ הַחַיּוּת הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִמֶּנּוּ; רַק כַּוָּנַת הַמְּנוּחָה וְסִלּוּק הַטְּרָדוֹת וְהַצַּעַר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נַפְשׁוֹ בְּנִיחָא לִדָּבֵק בְּקוֹנָהּ, שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּשֶׁיֵּשׁ דְּבָרִים הַמַּטְרִידִים הַלֵּב וּמְבַלְבְּלִים הָאָדָם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (ס״ה עַמּוּד א׳): "אִי קְרָצַתַּן כִּנָּה לָא תָּנָאֵי", וְעַל זֶה הוּא צֹרֶךְ נִיחָא דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה].
records.targetEnglish: (The intention is not bodily tranquility alone or enjoyment of this world’s delights. That certainly is not life, and the Torah is not speaking of the dead—those called dead even while alive. In Tamid: “What should a person do and live? Put himself to death. What should a person do and die? Keep himself alive.” Only one attached to God is called alive, as it says, “You who cling to the Lord your God are all alive.” A person is called alive only when life is attached to him and is not separated. Concerning “the son of a living man,” the sages say that the righteous are called living even in death. This is what is simply called life: there is no life except that drawn from the Life of the worlds, as it says, “You give life to them all.” Apart from this there is no life; as He endures forever, so does the life drawn from Him. The purpose of rest and the removal of troubles and suffering in this world is for the soul to be at ease and attach itself to its Maker. This is impossible when things trouble the heart and confuse the person, as they said in Eruvin: “If a louse had bitten me, I would not have learned.” It is for this that rest in this world is needed.)
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim specifies what rest makes possible: attachment becomes a life the person can actually experience when the heart is no longer consumed by disturbance. This explains why the Chanukah passage locates the establishment of holiness in the rest following the battle. Its explicit distinction from bodily comfort keeps the connection focused on dedication and inward settlement.

records.targetHebrew: ולזה תקנו לאמרו בחשאי, היינו אמת הוא שבעומק הלב של ישראל נמצא הבהירות מיעאע"ה וממעמד הר סיני, אכן לא יסמוך אדם להשען על זה, אך להתנהג מצידו בעבודה מיד בלי הפסק, ואז יגיע להכיר המראה הגדול גם בתפיסתו את הבהירות של יחודא עלאה, וזה נקרא בחשאי.
records.targetEnglish: Therefore they instituted saying it quietly. It is true that deep within Israel’s heart there is the clarity inherited from our father Jacob and from the standing at Mount Sinai. Yet a person must not rely on this and rest upon it. On his side he must conduct himself in service immediately and without interruption; then he will come to recognize, within his own perception as well, the great vision and clarity of the upper unity. This is called “quietly.”
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why the inherited light of upper unity does not cancel the work represented by lower unity: the person must acquire conscious recognition through actual service. That gives the twenty-four-to-twenty-five movement here an inward structure. The rest after the Chanukah victory is an attainment reached through the work, rather than permission to presume that the hidden root makes further work unnecessary.

records.originEnglish: “The Lord is one” indicates that everything is for the good, for this name indicates mercy and a desire only to benefit. In this world this is not revealed so that people recognize the good in its apparent opposite as well; that will be revealed only “on that day.” In the days of the Hasmoneans they attained rest in the aspect of upper unity. They all recognized that the decree had been for their benefit, since through it they defeated the Greeks and cast off their yoke. Only because the decree sought to turn them from their religion did they put themselves at risk of death to fight him; the miracle occurred, and they cast his yoke from their necks. This is the allusion to the twenty-five letters of upper unity in Tikkunei Zohar. Likewise, regarding Shabbat it says, “On the day the Lord gives you rest from your sorrow, your turmoil, and the hard service,” which is interpreted of Shabbat, the day of rest. It contains a revelation of the light created on the first day, of which it says, “God saw the light, that it was good.” Then one merits to apprehend that everything is for the good. Even while still within hard service, one has rest, because it is for the good. The holy Zohar likewise says, “For good will come—this is the resurrection of the dead; that destined light will shine.” Through the revelation of the first light, one merits to apprehend the true good.

records.targetEnglish: This is the joy a person should have in his service, as it says, “Serve the Lord with joy.” Although one must also have fear—“rejoice with trembling”—this joy too must never leave his sight: he has merited to serve God. Is there any greater joy? The righteous act from love and rejoice in sufferings as well, since they recognize that everything comes from God and is not chance, Heaven forbid. It is like a father striking his son to set him straight, or a physician doing painful things to a patient in order to preserve his life. Although the patient is distressed now, he certainly rejoices afterward. One who understands and recognizes this even while it is happening is joyful.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla explains the precise change that can bring inward rest before hardship has ended: the person recognizes its corrective purpose, like the patient who understands the treatment. It preserves both distress and awe rather than claiming that the experience has become physically pleasant. This illuminates the sentence that one can have rest even within hard service.
